items.item: The RAM model: a single processor, uniform memory of cells S[0], S[1], ..., a constant number of registers, and every instruction (load, store, arithmetic, jump) costs one time step; running time = number of instructions executed. [https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/Introduction.pdf]

at.step: The machine behind the count

items.item: Word-size convention: a cell holds a w-bit word with w >= log n (usually w >= log S for space S), because a word must be able to hold a pointer/array index; integers polynomial in the input size fit in O(1) words. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L11.pdf]

at.step: A word must hold a pointer: w ≥ log₂ n

items.item: Why words must be bounded: with unbounded unit-cost integers, n repeated squarings build a 2^n-bit number in n steps, giving absurdly optimistic algorithms (and P = NP with multiplication and shifts), so the word size is tied to the input size. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0210006]

at.step: A word must hold a pointer: w ≥ log₂ n

items.item: Big numbers are not unit cost: an integer of k bits occupies about k/w words and arithmetic on it costs time growing with k/w; spreading a value over logarithmically many cells costs only a logarithmic overhead, which is why constant-size and log-size cell models are interchangeable up to that factor. [https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/Introduction.pdf]

at.step: Big numbers pay by the word

items.item: Transdichotomous RAM (Fredman-Willard): the word size scales with the problem size, w >= log n, and a fixed set of operations each touching O(1) cells; words double as pointers, so memory is addressed arbitrarily. [https://classes.csail.mit.edu/6.851/fall17/scribe/lec11.pdf]

Unit-cost operations on the word RAM are the C-style ones: + - * / % & | ^ << >> and comparisons, each O(1) on a w-bit word; this is the standard model for integer data structures. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L11.pdf]

at.step: The machine behind the count

items.item: Multiplication is the contested operation: it is not in AC0 (needs depth growing with w), so the AC0 RAM allows only addition, shifts and bitwise ops; fusion trees rely heavily on multiplication, and AC0-only search results are weaker. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0210006]

at.deep: Which operations are unit cost is a choice

items.item: The RAM's key power over the comparison model: it can use keys to compute addresses (indexing, bucketing, bit extraction), which is exactly what bucket and radix sort exploit. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0210006]

at.step: On the word-RAM, a key is a number

at.deep: The comparison model and its escapes

items.item: Integer keys cover more than integers: floating-point numbers order correctly when their bit patterns are read as integers (for negatives the bits must be flipped first, a detail the source leaves out), so integer-key algorithms apply to many other key types. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0210006]

at.quote: key normalization of multi-column keys to byte strings

items.item: Comparison-sorting lower bound: any comparison-based sort needs n log n - O(n) comparisons worst case and on average; it cannot be broken within that model, only by enlarging the set of basic operations. [https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/SortingAndSelection.pdf]

at.quote: decision-tree Ω(n log n) for comparison sorting

at.step: The comparison model: one bit per question

items.item: Counting/bucket sort (KSort) sorts n keys in 0..K-1 in O(n + K) and is stable; LSD radix sort applies it digit by digit for keys in 0..K^d - 1 in O(d(n + K)), relying on stability for correctness. [https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/SortingAndSelection.pdf]

at.step: Radix sort: digits as addresses

items.item: Radix sort on the word RAM: with digit size log n bits, w-bit keys sort in O(n * w / log n) time, i.e. linear when w = O(log n); counting sort alone is O(n + 2^w). [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L14.pdf]

at.step: Radix sort: digits as addresses

items.item: State of integer sorting: signature sort is linear for w = Omega(log^(2+eps) n); Han gives O(n log log n) deterministic; Han-Thorup O(n sqrt(log log n)) randomized; whether O(n) sorting is possible for all w is open. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L14.pdf]

Thorup's equivalence: sorting n w-bit integers in O(n S(n,w)) time yields a priority queue with O(S(n,w)) per operation, so integer sorting and integer priority queues are tied. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L14.pdf]

Predecessor problem: maintain a set of integers from universe U = {0..u-1} under insert/delete and find predecessor/successor; it requires Theta(log n) in the BST/comparison model, which integer structures beat. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L11.pdf]

items.item: van Emde Boas trees: recursive sqrt(u) split into clusters plus a summary, min stored non-recursively so each operation recurses once: T(u) = T(sqrt u) + O(1) = O(log log u) = O(log w). [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L11.pdf]

at.step: van Emde Boas: halve the bits, not the keys

at.deep: van Emde Boas trees in full

items.item: vEB space is Theta(u), not Theta(n); replacing cluster arrays with dynamic perfect hash tables (storing only non-empty clusters) brings space to Theta(n) with O(log log u) bounds holding with high probability. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L11.pdf]

at.step: The price: Θ(U) space, unless you hash

at.deep: van Emde Boas trees in full

items.item: x-fast and y-fast tries (Willard): a hash table of all prefixes of stored keys allows binary search on prefix length in O(log w); indirection with Theta(w)-size BST buckets gives y-fast tries O(log w) operations in O(n) space. [https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.851/spring12/scribe/L11.pdf]

at.deep: van Emde Boas trees in full

items.item: Word-RAM hashing is itself a word-level trick: multiply-shift hashing (multiply by a random odd word, keep the high bits) is universal up to a factor 2 and far faster than mod-prime hashing; vEB/y-fast space bounds depend on such hashing. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1504.06804]

Fusion trees (Fredman-Willard): a B-tree of branching factor w^(1/5) where each node's keys are sketched into one word and compared in parallel, giving predecessor in O(log_w n) time with O(n) space. [https://classes.csail.mit.edu/6.851/fall17/scribe/lec12.pdf]

at.step: Fusion trees: four comparisons in one subtraction

at.deep: Fusion trees: the idea, and what is left out

items.item: Fusion-tree ingredients are word-level parallelism: sketching (compressing keys to their distinguishing bits via multiplication), parallel comparison of many small fields in one word, and computing the most significant set bit in O(1). [https://classes.csail.mit.edu/6.851/fall17/scribe/lec12.pdf]

at.step: Fusion trees: four comparisons in one subtraction

at.deep: Fusion trees: the idea, and what is left out

items.item: Combining vEB and fusion trees gives O(min{log w, log_w n}), which is at most O(sqrt(log n)); exponential search trees make this dynamic, reaching the optimal O(sqrt(log n / log log n)) worst case in linear space. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0210006]

at.deep: The comparison model and its escapes

items.item: Cell-probe model (Yao): memory of w-bit cells, only reads/writes cost, computation is free; it is stronger than the word RAM, so its lower bounds hold for any RAM algorithm. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0603043]

Predecessor lower bounds: with polynomial space, Omega(min{log_w n, log w / log log n}) cell probes are needed (Beame-Fich, round elimination), and Patrascu-Thorup give the exact time-space trade-off, so vEB and fusion trees are essentially optimal. [https://classes.csail.mit.edu/6.851/fall17/scribe/lec13.pdf]

Predecessor and external memory: the fusion-tree branch log_w n matches B-tree behaviour, and with cells of B keys the optimum is either a B-tree or the best RAM structure (Patrascu-Thorup). [https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0603043]

What unit cost hides, memory: a RAM has uniform memory, a real machine a hierarchy; a main-memory access can cost hundreds of times a cache hit, so operation costs are not fixed. [https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/Introduction.pdf]

at.step: One load, two prices

items.item: What unit cost hides, address translation: TLB misses force page-table walks; access patterns touching many pages slow down even when cache-line counts are equal. [https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf]

What unit cost hides, branch mispredictions: data-dependent comparisons (e.g. in quicksort partitioning) cause mispredictions that dominate running time; separating control flow from data flow speeds sorting by over 80%. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.06697]

at.step: A wrong guess flushes the pipeline

items.item: Branch-free and prefetch-friendly search: conditional moves and the Eytzinger layout make comparison search much faster in practice than layouts with the same RAM cost. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05053]

at.quote: branchless binary search with conditional moves

items.item: What unit cost hides, SIMD and instruction-level parallelism: 128-512-bit vector registers process many items per instruction (e.g. AVX2 popcount up to twice as fast as the scalar popcnt instruction); the word RAM models only one w-bit word per step. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.07612]

What unit cost hides, parallelism: multicore, SMT, GPUs and distributed systems; the sequential RAM gives no single simple model for these. [https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/Introduction.pdf]

What unit cost hides, memory allocation: malloc/free are treated as O(1) but real allocators trade locality, contention and fast paths, and allocator choice measurably changes performance. [https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2019/06/mimalloc-tr-v1.pdf]

Real-world relevance: in-place radix sort (IPS2Ra) wins on near-uniform keys and small keys, yet a tuned branchless comparison samplesort (IPS4o) often beats integer sorters, so asymptotic wins over the comparison model depend on the hidden costs. [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.13569]
